events.title: Telegram
events.text:
Ukraine is losing jets to its own missiles. 
Soviet-era R-60s from the 1960s are exploding on launch, says Come Back Alive chief Taras Chmut. 
Chmut said Ukraine lacks modern short-range air-to-air missiles like the AIM-9 Sidewinder, forcing pilots to use Cold War–era R-60s and R-73s against Russian drones and cruise missiles. 
"It's an old Soviet missile from the 60s that can explode at the moment of launch. And there have been such cases — we have lost several planes because of this." 
A confirmed case: a MiG-29 crashed near Odesa on 10 August 2026 after catching fire during missile launch on an anti-drone mission — the pilot ejected injured but alive. 
Chmut said there is "currently no alternative."

A U.S. Army exercise involving 9,700 soldiers in California exposed major shortcomings in its push toward AI-powered warfare.
Drones overheated, batteries failed, communications broke down, and experimental equipment struggled. Some drones operated without AI or autonomous capabilities.
Despite billions spent on modernization, the Army continues to struggle with unreliable technology, bureaucratic delays and outdated systems.
Officials acknowledged the setbacks but said improvements in communications, AI-assisted planning and data sharing were showing progress.
Source: WSJ

💵 Pentagon taps Raytheon for $6.3B interceptor refill after Iran war drains stocks
The failed US war gambit against Iran has left the Pentagon facing a costly race to replenish its missile defenses.
Raytheon has landed a $6.3B five-year contract to supply SM-3 Block IB interceptors. The Center for Strategic and International Studies listed the SM-3 Block IB among seven critical munitions facing supply concerns, alongside Patriot and THAAD interceptors, and Tomahawk cruise missiles.
The SM-3 Block IB deal was one of five framework agreements Raytheon signed with the Pentagon in February.
The rush to replenish drained stocks comes as national security experts and defense analysts warned that the US military's heavy use of missile interceptors against Iran risks depleting critical defensive capabilities if the conflict drags on.

events.text:
Who stands to gain from sabotaging Syria’s energy ambitions?
Just as Syria is promoting itself as a potential corridor for Iraqi oil and regional gas flows to the Mediterranean, a string of [suspicious attacks](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75415) has targeted its energy infrastructure.
🔶 On Aug. 18, an explosion halted gas pumping from the Jbessa plant in Hasakah 
🔶 On Sept. 28, another blast struck the Jbessa line near Al-Shula, Deir Ezzor
🔶 On Sept. 30, an explosion knocked the Tishreen, Deir Ali and Al-Nasiriyah power plants offline
The strikes coincide with Syria’s push to expand the Arab Gas Pipeline - a newly inaugurated section at Al-Furqlus adds capacity toward 11 million cubic meters per day - and revive the [Kirkuk–Baniyas](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73269) oil route.
➡️ such corridors could offer alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz, open direct path to European markets, lowering transit costs 
➡️ the corridors would compete with Israeli gas exports from Leviathan, Tamar, and Karish
➡️ Israel, which has [increased brash incursions ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/75054)and [strikes on Syria](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74885) since the fall of Assad, stands to gain from a weaker Syrian state 
➡️ ISIS remnants remain another possibility, given past infrastructure attacks
The strikes come as Syria under interim leader Ahmed Al-Sharaa slides deeper [into instability](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74728?single), gripped by armed clashes, targeted killings, and mounting protests over soaring fuel prices and living costs.
